solution.concept_anchor: Karakoram Pass vs Khyber Pass — precise location distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Khyber Pass connected to 'Ladakh-Xinjiang trade' sounds geographically adjacent to the Karakoram region; students unfamiliar with precise pass locations may accept it.
elimination_logic: Check option (a): Khyber Pass connects Afghanistan and Pakistan — it does NOT connect Ladakh and Xinjiang; this is a geographic-swap with the Karakoram Pass — incorrect.

Check option (b): Karakoram Pass is in the Karakoram range on the Ladakh-Xinjiang border — correct location; but calling it a 'gateway to the Indian subcontinent used by historic invaders' is wrong — that role belongs to Khyber/Bolan — incorrect pairing.

Check option (c): Bolan Pass connects Pakistan's Balochistan to Afghanistan — it is indeed distinct from the Khyber Pass (which is further north, in the NWFP/KP region) and served as a separate invasion/trade corridor — correctly matched.
Check option (d): Nathu La connects Sikkim to Tibet, not Kashmir to Pakistan — incorrect.
Option (c) is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Karakoram Pass vs Khyber Pass confusion is a classic UPSC trap: both are in the northwestern subcontinent's mountain zone, both are historically significant, but they serve completely different geographic connections. Karakoram Pass (Ladakh-Xinjiang) is a high-altitude trade route, while Khyber (Afghanistan-Pakistan) is the historic invasion corridor. Option (a) exploits this by assigning Khyber's trade description to Ladakh-Xinjiang geography.
solution.final_explanation:
Precise pass-location matching is a recurring UPSC test area. The northwestern subcontinental passes are often confused.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Khyber Pass connects Afghanistan and Pakistan (Peshawar-Jalalabad), not Ladakh and Xinjiang. That is the Karakoram Pass.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Karakoram Pass (Ladakh-Xinjiang) correctly located, but its description as 'gateway used by historic invaders into the subcontinent' is wrong — Khyber and Bolan served that role.
• Option (c) — Correct: Bolan Pass connects Balochistan (Pakistan) to Afghanistan and is a distinct, southerly invasion/trade corridor separate from the Khyber Pass, which runs through the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa region further north.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Nathu La connects Sikkim to Tibet (China), not Kashmir to Pakistan.

Value Addition:
• Bolan Pass was used by the British during the Anglo-Afghan Wars as an alternative to the Khyber route.
• The Karakoram Highway (KKH) follows an ancient Silk Route path but does not go through the Karakoram Pass — it crosses through the Khunjerab Pass.
• Khunjerab Pass (4,693 m) is the highest paved international border crossing in the world, connecting Pakistan and China.

solution.concept_anchor: African mountain types — fold vs volcanic vs rift-block

statement_analysis.statement: Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya are free-standing volcanic peaks, not part of any continuous fold mountain range, and their formation is linked to the East African Rift System.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Kilimanjaro (Tanzania) and Mount Kenya are isolated stratovolcanoes associated with the rift-related magmatic activity of the East African Rift System — they are not part of a fold mountain belt.

statement_analysis.statement: The Atlas Mountains of North Africa are part of the Great Rift Valley geology and were formed by the same tensional forces responsible for the East African Rift System.
statement_analysis.reason: The Atlas Mountains are fold mountains belonging to the Alpine-Himalayan orogenic belt, formed by the convergence of the African and Eurasian plates — they have no connection to the tensional East African Rift System.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ethiopian Highlands are described as the 'water tower of Africa' primarily because they are the source of the Blue Nile, among other rivers, and receive high orographic rainfall.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ethiopian Highlands receive high rainfall from orographic lifting of Indian Ocean moisture; the Blue Nile (Abbay River) originates from Lake Tana in these highlands and carries the majority of the Nile's water volume.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) selecting only statement 3 appeals to students who doubt Statement 1 (thinking Kilimanjaro is 'in a mountain range') and incorrectly accept Statement 2 as true due to the Atlas-Rift conflation.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Kilimanjaro and Kenya are rift-related volcanic peaks, not fold mountain range components — correct.
Verify Statement 2: Atlas = Alpine-Himalayan fold belt (African-Eurasian convergence), NOT East African Rift tectonics — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Ethiopian Highlands as Blue Nile source and Africa's 'water tower' — this is standard geographic knowledge; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the core conflation trap: both the Atlas and the East African Rift System are African tectonic features, and students who loosely associate 'African mountains = rift geology' will accept Statement 2 without distinguishing North African fold tectonics from East African rift tectonics. The UPSC has repeatedly tested this distinction because it requires understanding that different parts of Africa have fundamentally different tectonic histories.
solution.final_explanation:
Africa contains three fundamentally different types of mountain-forming processes operating in different regions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Kilimanjaro (Tanzania, 5,895 m) and Mount Kenya (Kenya, 5,199 m) are both volcanic peaks associated with the East African Rift's magmatic activity — not parts of any fold mountain belt.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Atlas Mountains formed through compression (African-Eurasian convergence), not through the tensional rifting that created the East African Rift System. These are geologically opposite processes.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Ethiopian Highlands receive high rainfall and generate the Blue Nile (which contributes ~80% of the Nile's total water) and the Awash River — earning the 'water tower of Africa' designation.

Value Addition:
• The White Nile originates from Lake Victoria (East Africa) — the Blue Nile brings the majority of the Nile's volume and sediment.
• The East African Rift is splitting Africa apart — the Somali Plate is slowly separating from the African Plate.
• The Rwenzori Mountains (Uganda-DRC border) are block mountains (horsts) within the East African Rift system — distinct from both volcanic peaks and fold mountains.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Nanga Parbat (8,126 m) is located at the western end of the Himalayas/Karakoram transition zone in Pakistan; students unfamiliar with its precise range assignment may select it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: All options are peaks above 8,000 m — the shared attribute being tested is whether they are in the Himalayan-Karakoram system.
Lhotse (8,516 m) — in the Himalayas (Nepal), adjacent to Everest — Himalayan-Karakoram system.

Option (b) Aconcagua is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is subtle: all four options are famous, high-elevation mountains mentioned in UPSC-level geography. Aconcagua is the second-highest mountain by some loose framing if students misremember the 'highest outside Asia' fact. The question tests whether students know that ALL peaks above 8,000 m are in the Himalayan-Karakoram system — Aconcagua at 6,961 m is far below that threshold and belongs to an entirely different continental range.
solution.final_explanation:

• Option (c) — Nanga Parbat: 8,126 m; ninth highest globally; located in the western Himalayan range in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan.
• Option (d) — Broad Peak: 8,051 m; twelfth highest globally; located in the Karakoram range on the Pakistan-China border.

Value Addition:
• Nanga Parbat's south face ('Rupal Face') is the highest rock face on Earth.
• Aconcagua's name derives from the Quechua language — 'stone sentinel.'
• The 14 eight-thousanders span Nepal, Tibet (China), Pakistan, and India.

solution.concept_anchor: Andes countries traversed — seven nations
solution.strong_distractor: c — '6 countries' sounds plausible because fewer well-known South American countries are associated with the Andes; students may forget one of the seven (often Venezuela or Ecuador).
elimination_logic: The Andes run the entire length of South America's western coast — identify the countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina.
Count: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina = 7 countries.
Eliminate options citing 5 or 6 countries — the precise number is seven.
Option (a) — 7 countries — is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap here is actually a count-swap: students frequently undercount Andes countries because they associate the range primarily with its most prominent Andean nations (Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina) and forget Venezuela and Ecuador at the northern end and sometimes confuse whether Brazil has Andean territory (it does not — Brazil's highlands are the Planalto, separate). The precise count of seven is regularly tested.
solution.final_explanation:
The Andes Mountains are the world's longest continental mountain range, running approximately 7,000 km along South America's western edge from Venezuela in the north to Tierra del Fuego in the south.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Andes pass through seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina — the complete and accurate count.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Five countries would exclude Venezuela and Colombia (or other northern nations).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Six is the most common wrong answer — students typically omit one country, most often Venezuela.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Eight would require adding a country not part of the Andean chain; Brazil, for instance, is a common wrongly added country.

Value Addition:
• Brazil does NOT have Andean territory — its highlands are the Brazilian Planalto (ancient shield rocks).
• The Andes reach their greatest elevation in Argentina (Aconcagua, 6,961 m).
• Bolivia and Peru share Lake Titicaca, the world's highest navigable lake (3,812 m), in the Altiplano between the Andean cordilleras.

solution.concept_anchor: Alpine-Himalayan fold belt — plate collisions generating each range
solution.strong_distractor: a — Swapping the Arabian-Eurasian collision (Zagros) with African-Eurasian collision (Alps/Atlas) is the primary trap; students who know 'African plate creates Alpine ranges' may misassign it to Zagros.
elimination_logic: Alps: formed by collision of African and Eurasian plates — matches with 2.
Zagros: formed by collision of Arabian Plate and Eurasian Plate — matches with 4.
Atlas: formed by convergence of African and Eurasian plates (same as Alps but in North Africa) — matches with 1.
Himalayas: formed by collision of Indian Plate (part of Indo-Australian) and Eurasian Plate — matches with 3.
Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap conflates the African-Eurasian collision (which created both the Alps and the Atlas) with the Arabian-Eurasian collision (which created the Zagros). Students who know 'African plate = Alpine orogeny' may extend this to the Zagros without recognising that the Arabian Plate, though adjacent to Africa, is a separate plate unit. The Atlas-Alps sharing the same collision type is an additional subtlety — both are African-Eurasian, but the Atlas is in North Africa and the Alps in Europe.
solution.final_explanation:
All four ranges are part of the Alpine-Himalayan fold mountain belt but were created by different specific plate collisions.

• A (Alps) — Matches with 2 (African-Eurasian collision): The African Plate's northward movement into the Eurasian Plate created the Alps in southern Europe.
• B (Zagros) — Matches with 4 (Arabian-Eurasian collision): The Arabian Plate, separate from the African Plate, converges northward into Eurasia, creating the Zagros fold-and-thrust belt in Iran and Iraq.
• C (Atlas) — Matches with 1 (African-Eurasian in North Africa): Same collision type as Alps but expressed in North Africa — the African Plate's convergence creates the Atlas ranges.
• D (Himalayas) — Matches with 3 (Indian-Eurasian collision): The northward movement of the Indian Plate into Eurasia since ~50 Ma created the Himalayas.

Value Addition:
• The Arabian Plate is slowly closing the Persian Gulf and squeezing Iran between it and the Eurasian Plate.
• The Taurus Mountains (Turkey) are also formed by African-Eurasian convergence — part of the same belt as the Zagros.
• The Zagros oil deposits are in anticlinal traps — folded rock layers that trap petroleum.

solution.concept_anchor: Block mountains — Vosges, Black Forest, Sierra Nevada USA correctly classified

statement_analysis.statement: Vosges Mountains (France) — Block mountain (horst)
statement_analysis.reason: The Vosges are a classic horst, uplifted as the Rhine Graben (rift valley) formed between them and the Black Forest on the opposite bank.

statement_analysis.statement: Black Forest (Germany) — Block mountain (horst)
statement_analysis.reason: The Schwarzwald (Black Forest) is the eastern horst corresponding to the Vosges to the west — both were uplifted as the Rhine Graben formed through tensional faulting.

statement_analysis.statement: Sierra Nevada (Spain) — Block mountain (horst)
statement_analysis.reason: The Sierra Nevada in Spain is a fold mountain (part of the Betic Cordillera), formed by the convergence of the African and Eurasian plates — it is NOT a block mountain, unlike the Sierra Nevada in the USA which is a tilted fault block.

statement_analysis.statement: Rwenzori Mountains (Uganda-DRC) — Block mountain (horst)
statement_analysis.reason: The Rwenzori (Mountains of the Moon) are a horst block uplifted between the western branches of the East African Rift — a textbook example of a rift-related block mountain in Africa.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' tempts students who know Vosges, Black Forest, and Rwenzori as block mountains and assume the Sierra Nevada (Spain) follows the same pattern as the Sierra Nevada (USA).
elimination_logic: Vosges (France) — classic Rhine Graben horst — correctly classified as block mountain.
Black Forest (Germany) — corresponding horst on the other side of the Rhine Graben — correctly classified.
Sierra Nevada (Spain) — Betic Cordillera fold mountain; NOT a block mountain — incorrectly classified in this pairing.
Rwenzori (Uganda-DRC) — East African Rift horst block mountain — correctly classified.
Three correct, one incorrect — answer is option (c) — Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Sierra Nevada (Spain) vs Sierra Nevada (USA) conflation is one of the most reliable UPSC geography traps. The Sierra Nevada in the USA (California) is a tilted fault block (block mountain). The Sierra Nevada in Spain (Andalusia) is a fold mountain in the Betic Cordillera, formed by African-Eurasian plate convergence. Students who correctly know the USA Sierra Nevada as a block mountain wrongly extend that classification to the Spanish range.
solution.final_explanation:
Block mountains (horsts) form when tensional forces create normal faults and crustal blocks between faults are uplifted relative to the surrounding graben (rift valley) blocks.

| Range | Claimed Type | Correct? |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Vosges (France) | Block mountain | Yes — Rhine Graben horst |
| Black Forest (Germany) | Block mountain | Yes — Rhine Graben horst |
| Sierra Nevada (Spain) | Block mountain | No — fold mountain (Betic Cordillera) |
| Rwenzori (Uganda-DRC) | Block mountain | Yes — East African Rift horst |

Value Addition:
• Sierra Nevada (USA, California) IS a tilted fault block — the key distinction from Sierra Nevada, Spain.
• The Betic Cordillera (Spain) is part of the same Alpine fold system as the Atlas and Apennines.
• The Rwenzori are sometimes called the 'Mountains of the Moon' — referenced by ancient geographers as the source of the Nile.

solution.concept_anchor: Alps vs Himalayas — climatic barrier comparison

statement_analysis.statement: The Himalayas function as a climatic barrier in two ways: they block the cold, dry Central Asian winds from entering the subcontinent in winter, and they trap the monsoon moisture on the southern slopes, preventing it from reaching the Tibetan Plateau.
statement_analysis.reason: Both functions are geographically accurate — the Himalayas prevent Central Asian cold air from reaching South Asia (maintaining warmer winters) and the windward southern slopes receive heavy monsoon rainfall while the leeward Tibetan side is arid.

statement_analysis.statement: The Alps similarly function as an effective monsoon-blocking barrier for Central Europe, preventing Atlantic moisture from penetrating into Eastern Europe during summer months.
statement_analysis.reason: The Alps do NOT create a monsoon-blocking effect comparable to the Himalayas. Central Europe does not have a monsoon system. The Alps influence local precipitation patterns (orographic rainfall, Foehn winds) but do not block or create monsoon systems — the comparison is false.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both statements appear to describe similar climatic barrier functions for the world's two greatest fold mountain systems; students may accept both as parallel truths without recognising that Central Europe has no monsoon to block.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Himalayas blocking cold Central Asian winds (winter) and trapping monsoon moisture (summer) — both are well-documented climatic functions — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Alps do not create or block a monsoon system in Central Europe — Europe's climate is governed by westerly winds and Atlantic influences, not a monsoon — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 borrows the Himalayan climatic barrier framework and incorrectly applies it to the Alps. Students who know 'mountains act as climatic barriers' may accept the Alps-monsoon comparison as a plausible analogy. The critical knowledge required is that monsoon systems are absent in Central Europe — the Alps influence orographic precipitation and Foehn winds, but the concept of 'monsoon blocking' simply does not apply.
solution.final_explanation:
The Himalayas are uniquely significant as a climatic barrier because South Asia has a monsoon climate system that interacts with the range in two documented ways.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Himalayas act as a dual barrier — blocking cold, dry Central Asian continental air from reaching South Asia in winter (keeping Indian winters milder than comparable latitudes), and trapping monsoon moisture on their windward southern slopes while leaving the Tibetan Plateau arid.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Central Europe does not have a monsoon system. The Alps influence local climate through orographic effects (rainfall on windward slopes, Foehn on leeward slopes) and act as a thermal divide, but there is no Atlantic 'monsoon' to block. Europe's moisture delivery is from persistent westerly winds, not seasonal monsoon circulation.

Value Addition:
• The Tibetan Plateau's arid cold-desert character (e.g., Aksai Chin) is a direct consequence of the Himalayan rain shadow.
• Mediterranean Europe does experience a distinct wet-dry seasonal pattern sometimes loosely called 'Mediterranean monsoon' — but this is not a monsoon in the meteorological sense.
• The Western Ghats of India create a rain shadow over the Deccan Plateau — a similar orographic mechanism on a smaller scale.

solution.concept_anchor: GLOFs and Karakoram anomaly — climate change linkage

statement_analysis.statement: Glacier Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) occur when the natural dam of a glacial lake — formed by moraine, ice, or bedrock — fails suddenly, releasing large volumes of water downstream.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard definition of a GLOF: the sudden failure of a glacial lake's dam (moraine, ice, or rock) releases stored water catastrophically into downstream valleys.

statement_analysis.statement: The Himalayan region — including parts of Uttarakhand, Nepal, and Bhutan — is among the most vulnerable zones for GLOFs globally, primarily because rapid glacier retreat is increasing the number and volume of proglacial lakes.
statement_analysis.reason: As Himalayan glaciers retreat, meltwater accumulates in moraine-dammed proglacial lakes, which are unstable and prone to catastrophic failure — Uttarakhand, Nepal, and Bhutan have experienced multiple GLOF events.

statement_analysis.statement: The Karakoram Anomaly refers to the phenomenon where all glaciers in the Karakoram range are advancing rapidly due to increased summer temperatures, which accelerate basal sliding of glaciers.
statement_analysis.reason: The Karakoram Anomaly is the phenomenon of some (not all) Karakoram glaciers being stable or advancing — this is attributed to increased winter precipitation (westerly disturbances), not increased summer temperatures or basal sliding. Summer warming would accelerate melting, not advancement.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All three options appear individually plausible; Statement 3 sounds like a scientific explanation for glacier advancement and the 'Karakoram Anomaly' is a real term, making the wrong mechanism hard to detect.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: GLOF definition — failure of glacial lake dam releasing water catastrophically — correct.
Verify Statement 2: Himalayan region (Uttarakhand, Nepal, Bhutan) GLOF vulnerability due to proglacial lake formation from glacier retreat — correct.

Verify Statement 3: Karakoram Anomaly involves some (not all) glaciers, and the mechanism is increased winter snowfall (westerly disturbances), not summer temperature increase — the statement reverses the mechanism — incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap on two levels: (1) 'all glaciers' vs 'some glaciers' — the anomaly applies to a subset, not uniformly; (2) the mechanism is inverted — increased summer temperatures would cause melting, not advancement; the actual driver is increased winter precipitation from westerly disturbances. Students who know the Karakoram Anomaly as a 'glacier advancement' phenomenon but not its specific mechanism will accept the plausible-sounding basal sliding explanation.
solution.final_explanation:
Glacier dynamics in the Himalayan-Karakoram region are complex and have significant implications for water security and disaster risk.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A GLOF occurs when a glacial lake's natural dam fails, releasing large volumes of water in a sudden flood — a well-defined glaciological hazard.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Himalayan region is a GLOF hotspot; glacial retreat creates expanding moraine-dammed lakes prone to sudden failure. The 2013 Kedarnath disaster had GLOF elements; Nepal's Imja Lake is a monitored high-risk site.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Karakoram Anomaly involves some (not all) glaciers remaining stable or advancing. The mechanism is enhanced winter snowfall from westerly disturbances — not increased summer temperatures (which would cause melting, not advancement). Basal sliding is accelerated by warming, which is the opposite of what produces anomalous advancement.

Value Addition:
• ISRO and other agencies have mapped over 5,000 glacial lakes in the Indian Himalayan region.
• The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) has issued guidelines for GLOF risk assessment.
• The Gangotri Glacier has retreated over 22 km since 1780 — one of India's most-cited climate change indicators.

solution.concept_anchor: Pamir as plateau convergence point — not a standard mountain range
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may verify both A (Pamir as 'Roof of the World') and R (ranges radiating from Pamir) as correct facts and assume they are causally linked without examining whether the nickname itself is caused by the range convergence or by the altitude.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? The Pamirs are called the 'Roof of the World' because of their extreme altitude (averaging 4,000–7,000 m) — A is correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The Himalayas, Karakoram, Hindukush, Tian Shan, and Kunlun do all radiate from the Pamir Knot — R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The nickname 'Roof of the World' refers to the Pamirs' extraordinary elevation — a function of altitude. The convergence of ranges is a geographic fact about the Pamir Knot, but R reverses the causation: the ranges do not radiate FROM the Pamirs because they are the 'Roof of the World' — rather, the Pamirs are the 'Roof' because of altitude, and the range convergence is a separate fact. R does not causally explain why the Pamirs are called 'Roof of the World.'
Both A and R correct but R does NOT explain A — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap: both facts are true and geographically related, so students will accept option (a). But the causal link is not there — the 'Roof of the World' designation is about altitude, not about being a convergence point. The ranges radiating from the Pamir Knot explains the Pamir's geographic centrality, not its 'Roof of the World' nickname. A student who reads R as an explanation for A without checking the actual causal mechanism will choose (a) incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The Pamirs occupy one of Earth's most extraordinary geographic positions — a high-altitude plateau at the convergence of five major mountain systems.

Assertion (A): Correct — The Pamirs' 'Roof of the World' designation reflects their extreme elevation (plateau average ~4,000–7,000 m), making them among the highest plateaus on Earth.
Reason (R): Correct — The Himalayas, Karakoram, Hindukush, Tian Shan, and Kunlun do radiate outward from the Pamir Knot — this is geographically accurate.
Causal link: The nickname 'Roof of the World' is a function of altitude, not of serving as a convergence point. R describes the Pamir's geographic role as a range-junction but does not explain why the altitude earns this specific designation. The two facts are independently true but causally unrelated.

Correct answer: (b)

Value Addition:
• The Pamir is a plateau, not a single mountain range — 'Pamir Knot' is a geographic concept, not a named peak.
• The Pamirs are shared among Tajikistan, Afghanistan, China, and Kyrgyzstan.
• Ismoil Somoni Peak (7,495 m) in Tajikistan's Pamir is the highest point in the former Soviet Union.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Assertion (A): The Pamir Plateau in Central Asia is known as the 'Roof of the World' owing to its extraordinary high elevation, with average altitudes ranging between 4,000 and 7,000 metres above sea level.

Reason (R): Several of Asia's greatest mountain systems — including the Himalayas, Karakoram, Hindukush, Tian Shan, and Kunlun — radiate outward from the Pamir Knot, making it the geographic convergence point of these ranges.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
